# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/main/interchain-token-service/contracts/utils/InterchainTokenDeployer.sol#L37-L6


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `InterchainTokenDeployer` contract uses the `Create3Fixed` contract to deploy new instances of the `InterchainTokenProxy` contract. However, it does not verify if the bytecode of the implementation contract has changed before deploying new proxy contracts. This can lead to a situation where newly deployed proxies continue to point to an outdated implementation contract, resulting in unexpected behavior and potential inconsistencies across the deployed proxy contracts.

## Proof of Concept

The issue arises in the following scenario:

1. An initial implementation contract is deployed and its address is used by the `InterchainTokenDeployer` contract.
2. Multiple `InterchainTokenProxy` contracts are deployed, all pointing to this initial implementation.
3. Later, a new implementation contract is deployed (e.g., to upgrade the token logic or fix a bug).
4. The `InterchainTokenDeployer` continues to deploy new proxies pointing to the old implementation, as it does not check whether the implementation address has changed.

This results in a mixed environment where older proxies point to the outdated implementation, and any new proxies deployed with the same deployment logic also point to the outdated implementation. The new implementation is effectively ignored unless manually updated, leading to potential discrepancies in contract behavior.

```solidity
function deployInterchainToken(
    bytes32 salt,
    bytes32 tokenId,
    address minter,
    string calldata name,
    string calldata symbol,
    uint8 decimals
) external returns (address tokenAddress) {
    ...
    // Proxies will continue to point to the old implementation unless checked and updated
    address implementation = implementationAddress;
    ...
    // New proxy contracts are deployed, but no verification is done to ensure the implementation is current
    tokenAddress = _create3(bytecode, salt);
    ...
}
```

## Tools Used

 Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps


- Add a mechanism to verify that the implementation contract's bytecode matches the expected version before deploying new proxy contracts.
- This could be done by storing a hash of the implementation's bytecode and comparing it with the current implementation's bytecode before deploying new proxies.



## Assessed type

Error

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L676-L687
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L375-L396


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`expressExecuteWithToken` and `expressExecute`  are used to transfer tokens to `destinationAddress` before `execute` are called on dest chain, and later when `execute` the tokens will be sent to the caller to repay the tokens.

## Proof of Concept
I will take [InterchainTokenService.expressExecute](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L375-L396) as an example, before sending tokens to `destinationAddress`, the only check `InterchainTokenService.expressExecute` perform is to make sure the `commandId` is not executed in [InterchainTokenService.sol#L386](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L386)
```solidity
 375     function expressExecute(
 376         bytes32 commandId,
 377         string calldata sourceChain,
 378         string calldata sourceAddress,
 379         bytes calldata payload
 380     ) public payable whenNotPaused {
	 ...
 385 
 386         if (gateway.isCommandExecuted(commandId)) revert AlreadyExecuted(); <<<--- The only check here to make sure `commandId` is not executed.
 387 
	 ...
 396     }
```

And based on onchain tx, the check is not sufficient.
I'll take onchain tx [0x14233d77b1b842ed2966f6e537f1138dc2e1e25a57cd18b5e9b6a9d073d30f8c](https://polygonscan.com/tx/0x14233d77b1b842ed2966f6e537f1138dc2e1e25a57cd18b5e9b6a9d073d30f8c) and [0xa2b449ef4f7ca209ce7d051c6a12f68433450bee6243a57c714e90a9c2fdcb03](https://polygonscan.com/tx/0xa2b449ef4f7ca209ce7d051c6a12f68433450bee6243a57c714e90a9c2fdcb03) as an example.

As show in [InterchainTokenService.sol#L386](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L386), when calling `InterchainTokenService.expressExecute` the function calls `if (gateway.isCommandExecuted(commandId)) revert AlreadyExecuted();` to make sure `commandId` hasn't been executed.
And then according to onchain [tx 0xa2b449ef4f7ca209ce7d051c6a12f68433450bee6243a57c714e90a9c2fdcb03](https://polygonscan.com/tx/0xa2b449ef4f7ca209ce7d051c6a12f68433450bee6243a57c714e90a9c2fdcb03), commandId(0xe0d17b56b8c9103330ceb9df8154d1585d8e92d3a0ef1b2858d7b783c7fab350) is set as executed in [block 60998951](https://polygonscan.com/tx/0xa2b449ef4f7ca209ce7d051c6a12f68433450bee6243a57c714e90a9c2fdcb03)
After that in [block 60998960 tx 0x14233d77b1b842ed2966f6e537f1138dc2e1e25a57cd18b5e9b6a9d073d30f8c](https://polygonscan.com/tx/0x14233d77b1b842ed2966f6e537f1138dc2e1e25a57cd18b5e9b6a9d073d30f8c), commandId(0xe0d17b56b8c9103330ceb9df8154d1585d8e92d3a0ef1b2858d7b783c7fab350) gets executed.

To sum up, in order to use `InterchainTokenService.expressExecute` successfully, Alice has to call `InterchainTokenService.expressExecute` before `block 60998951`(we will use **block 60998950** as example). And then in `block 60998951`, the Axelar Relayer calls `Axelar.Gateway.execute` to set the commandId(0xe0d17b56b8c9103330ceb9df8154d1585d8e92d3a0ef1b2858d7b783c7fab350) as executed. And finally, in `block 60998960`, `InterchainTokenService.execute` is called, in this function, token will sent to Alice instead of `destinationAddress`.

Now please consider reorg happens for polygon, the reorg depth can be [36 block](https://polygonscan.com/block/53035402/f?hash=0xba1e90f7bdc63880443e99ee63f38ec188c2c54cc994c6cca86bfe4b4c007af8).So please consider after reorg:
1. `InterchainTokenService.execute` is called in `block 60998950`
2. Alice calls `InterchainTokenService.expressExecute` in `block 60998951`
3. Axelar Relayer calls `Axelar.Gateway.execute` to set the commandId as executed in `block 60998960`

In such case, Alice's token will be stuck

## Proof of Concept
Take [GatewayCaller.callContractWithToken](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/utils/GatewayCaller.sol#L35-L69)

```solidity
 35     function callContract(
 36         string calldata destinationChain,
 37         string calldata destinationAddress,
 38         bytes calldata payload,
 39         MetadataVersion metadataVersion,
 40         uint256 gasValue
 41     ) external payable override {
 42         if (gasValue > 0) {
 43             if (metadataVersion == MetadataVersion.CONTRACT_CALL) {
 44                 // slither-disable-next-line arbitrary-send-eth
 45                 gasService.payNativeGasForContractCall{ value: gasValue }(
		 ...
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L172-L210


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
According to comments in [InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L165](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L165), `originalChainName means The name of the chain where the token originally exists`
However, `originalChainName` can only be set to **the only value** as `keccak256(bytes(originalChainName)) == InterchainTokenService.chainNameHash`, which means it can only be set to one value.

## Proof of Concept
While calling [InterchainTokenFactory.deployRemoteInterchainToken](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L172-L210), in [InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L192-L200](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L192-L200), the function calculates [tokenId](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L192-L194), and then get local `IInterchainToken token` based on `tokenId` in [InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L196](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L196), and then query token metadata in [InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L198-L200](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L198-L200).

In order to make sure [InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L198-L200](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L198-L200) won't revert, it means `IInterchainToken token` must be deployed in the local chain

And based on how [tokenId](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L192-L194) is calculated, it means that `IInterchainToken token` has to be deployed by [InterchainTokenFactory.deployInterchainToken](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L127-L161).
And in `InterchainTokenFactory.deployInterchainToken`, the `chainNameHash` is constant value set in [InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L42](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L42)

So to sum up, in `InterchainTokenFactory.deployRemoteInterchainToken`, the function use locally deployed `IInterchainToken` to fetch metadata(name/symbol/decimals), and because when deploy `IInterchainToken` token, `chainNameHash` uses constant value, so `originalChainName` in `InterchainTokenFactory.deployRemoteInterchainToken` can only be set to `chainNameHash`, otherwise, the function will revert in [InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L198](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L198)

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L454-L478
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L488-L511
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L527-L551


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Some tokens have different implementation on different chains. For example, [USDT](https://etherscan.io/token/0xdac17f958d2ee523a2206206994597c13d831ec7#writeContract#F6) has `pause` function on Eth, and doesn't have `pause` on [ploygonscan](https://polygonscan.com/token/0xc2132d05d31c914a87c6611c10748aeb04b58e8f#writeProxyContract). 
If such tokens are used, on the source chain, the token can be transferred as expect, but on the dest chain, the token is paused, which will lead the token be stuck in source chain.
## Proof of Concept
I'll take [InterchainTokenService.interchainTransfer](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L454-L478) as an example.
Suppose on Polygon, USDT(doesn't have `pause` function) is used, Alice calls `InterchainTokenService.interchainTransfer` to transfer USDT to Ethereum. But on Ethereum, USDT(which has `pause` function) is paused.

While Alice calls `InterchainTokenService.interchainTransfer` to transfer USDT from polygon to ethereum, in [InterchainTokenService.interchainTransfer](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L454-L478), the function doesn't check the USDT on ethereum has been paused, `interchainTransfer` calls `_takeToken` to transfer USDT from Alice, and compose a message which will be routed to ethereum.
And for `InterchainTokenService.execute` on the ethereum(dest chain), while calling `_giveToken`, the tx will be reverted because USDT is paused on ethereum.
In such case, the USDT on polygon will be stuck

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/gateway/BaseAmplifierGateway.sol#L115-L117


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`BaseAmplifierGateway.isCommandExecuted` isn't correct. 
Combining this function and `BaseAmplifierGateway.approveMessages`, a malicious signer can DOS `express execute operations` in some case.

## Proof of Concept
[BaseAmplifierGateway.isCommandExecuted](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/gateway/BaseAmplifierGateway.sol#L115-L117) has two issues.
First it doesn't consistent with [BaseAmplifierGateway.isMessageExecuted](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/gateway/BaseAmplifierGateway.sol#L75-L77)
```solidity
 75     function isMessageExecuted(string calldata sourceChain, string calldata messageId) external view returns (bool) {
 76         return _baseAmplifierGatewayStorage().messages[messageToCommandId(sourceChain, messageId)] == MESSAGE_EXECUTED; <<<--- check if message's state is MESSAGE_EXECUTED
 77     }
 ...
115     function isCommandExecuted(bytes32 commandId) public view override returns (bool) {
116         return _baseAmplifierGatewayStorage().messages[commandId] != MESSAGE_NONEXISTENT; <<<--- check if message's state is not MESSAGE_NONEXISTENT
117     }
```

Second, even though there are two states MESSAGE_EXECUTED and MESSAGE_NONEXISTENT defined, but there is another state `approved` as described in [BaseAmplifierGateway.sol#L15-L20](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/gateway/BaseAmplifierGateway.sol#L15-L20). 
And Because `isCommandExecuted` is used by `express execute operations` like [expressExecute](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/express/AxelarValuedExpressExecutable.sol#L131-L152) and [expressExecuteWithToken](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/express/AxelarValuedExpressExecutable.sol#L154-L204), a malicious signer might abusing this function and [AxelarAmplifierGateway.approveMessages](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/gateway/AxelarAmplifierGateway.sol#L80-L86) to DOS `express execute operations`

Please consider the following case:
1. Alice the malicious signer has enough weights for [BaseWeightedMultisig._validateSignatures](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/governance/BaseWeightedMultisig.sol#L192-L234) to be successful
2. Bob wants to run express execute operations to speed up some tx
3. Alice sees Bob's express operations in mempool, and she wants to DOS the tx
4. Alice front-run Bob's tx by calling [AxelarAmplifierGateway.approveMessages](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/gateway/AxelarAmplifierGateway.sol#L80-L86) to approve the message, because she has enough weights for `BaseWeightedMultisig._validateSignatures`, Alice's tx will success, and **the message's state will be set to APPROVED**
5. When Bob's express operation gets executed, the function will check if the message has been executed by calling `BaseAmplifierGateway.isCommandExecuted`, because the message's state is not `MESSAGE_NONEXISTENT`, Bob's tx will be reverted

## Tools Used
VS code
## Recommended Mitigation Steps


## Assessed type

title: TokenHandler:transferTokenFrom doesn't ensure msg.value is equal to the desired amount in case of tokenIds of native tokens
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L405


# Vulnerability details

## Description
In case a user wants to transfer native tokens across chains, the expressExecute function at the InterchainTokenService contract is payable and attempts to call TokenHandler's transferTokenFrom function. 
The logic, however, has some oversights:
The first one is the msg.value of the payable call. If a user wants to send some native tokens at the express execution, there should be sanity checks ensuring the payload-encoded amount corresponds to the msg.value. This doesn't happen at the `expressExecute` or at the `_expressExecute` implementations.

The second oversight is at the delegate call to  TokenHandler's transferTokenFrom function:
the `_expressExecute` function decodes the amount but never checks if the tokenId's corresponding token address is zero and doesn't check if the amount is equal to the msg.value:
```solidity
function _expressExecute(bytes32 commandId, string calldata sourceChain, bytes calldata payload) internal {
        (, bytes32 tokenId, bytes memory sourceAddress, bytes memory destinationAddressBytes, uint256 amount, bytes memory data) = abi
            .decode(payload, (uint256, bytes32, bytes, bytes, uint256, bytes));
       ...
            (bool success, bytes memory returnData) = tokenHandler.delegatecall(
                abi.encodeWithSelector(ITokenHandler.transferTokenFrom.selector, tokenId, msg.sender, destinationAddress, amount)
            );
    ...
}
```
## Impact
Malicious users may attempt to do native transfers with amounts set on the payload without sending any msg.value in order to spend the available InterchainTokenService native funds.
Legitimate users that want to help the protocol work by doing express executions may set amounts lower than the msg.value and not receive any sort of refund.

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Make sure the amount variable decoded at the payload is sanity checked in case the tokenId's corresponding token address is zero.
Make sure not to allow users to send a msg.value different than this amount.


## Assessed type

Context

raw_row.title: msg.value is decoupled from the gasValue parameter

title: msg.value is decoupled from the gasValue parameter
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L286
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenFactory.sol#L172


# Vulnerability details

## Description
The InterchainTokenFactory and InterchainTokenService contracts have a bridging payment logic on that decouples the msg.value from the desired payment amount.
Take a look at the deployRemoteInterchainToken function at the InterchainTokenFactory contract:
```solidity
function deployRemoteInterchainToken(
        string calldata originalChainName,
        bytes32 salt,
        address minter,
        string memory destinationChain,
        uint256 gasValue
    ) external payable returns (bytes32 tokenId) {
    ...
    tokenId = _deployInterchainToken(salt, destinationChain, tokenName, tokenSymbol, tokenDecimals, minter_, gasValue);
    }
```

It also happens at the deployTokenManager function at the InterchainTokenFactory contract:
```solidity
function deployTokenManager(
        bytes32 salt,
        string calldata destinationChain,
        TokenManagerType tokenManagerType,
        bytes calldata params,
        uint256 gasValue
    ) external payable whenNotPaused returns (bytes32 tokenId) {
    ...
    _deployRemoteTokenManager(tokenId, destinationChain, gasValue, tokenManagerType, params);
        }
    }
```
It doesn't sanity check msg.value, nor if it is worth at least the gasValue uint256.
## Impact
It is known the gateway will refund the excess payment made to bridge a message - if a user, however, sends a msg.value that is greater than gas value, he/she will not receive refunds for this difference.

Any native token left at the InterchainTokenService and at the InterchainTokenFactory contracts can be permissionless spent by any caller to pay for bridging a message. 
## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation
Make sure to sanity check if the gasValue uint256 variable is equal to the msg.value, otherwise revert. This option would be optimal if maintaining the function's interface is crucial.
A second option would be to remove the gasValue parameter altogether from the function and utilize the native msg.value as the accounting mechanism.


## Assessed type

ETH-Transfer

raw_row.title: The execute contract at the interchain-token-service doesn't initialize the token balance at the source chain when deploying an interchain token

title: The execute contract at the interchain-token-service doesn't initialize the token balance at the source chain when deploying an interchain token
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-amplifier/interchain-token-service/src/contract/execute.rs#L112


# Vulnerability details

## Description
In the context of interchain transfer messages, the apply_balance_tracking function firstly updates the token balance on the source chain by subtracting the amount sent from the stored value then adding this same amount to the token balance on the destination chain, as can be seen here:
```rust
update_token_balance(
                storage,
                token_id.clone(),
                source_chain.clone(),
                *amount,
                false,
            )
            .change_context_lazy(|| Error::BalanceUpdateFailed(source_chain, token_id.clone()))?;

            // Update the balance on the destination chain
            update_token_balance(
                storage,
                token_id.clone(),
                destination_chain.clone(),
                *amount,
                true,
            )
```

When deploying an interchain token, the token balance is initialized for the destination chain, but not for the source chain:
```rust
ItsMessage::DeployInterchainToken { token_id, .. } => {
            start_token_balance(storage, token_id.clone(), destination_chain.clone(), true)
                .change_context(Error::InvalidStoreAccess)?
        }
```

This is not entirely correct, as the interchain transfers will attempt remove stored balance from the source chain.  If the program initializes the source chain's balance to zero or not initialize the balance at all, interchain transfers will revert with overflow errors:
OverflowError::new(OverflowOperation::Sub) 
https://docs.rs/cosmwasm-std/latest/src/cosmwasm_std/math/uint256.rs.html#251-256

## Impact
Interchain transfers have a zero-day that stops them from being processed due to overflows on balance tracking logic.
## Proof of Concept
The tests artificially initialize the source chain balance in order to fit the program. Since the tests are not part of the programs logic, it is not possible to extrapolate such logic is reproducible in production.
In the tests, the update_token_balance function is called outside of the execute contract's functions:
```rust
 fn balance_tracking_interchain_transfer() {
 ...
 // Simulate an initial balance on the source chain
        state::update_token_balance(
            deps.as_mut().storage,
            token_id.clone(),
            source_chain.clone(),
            amount,
            true,
        )
        .unwrap();
...
}
```

As stated in the comment, this is to simulate an initial balance on the source chain. The execute contract, however, doesn't have a function that enables one-sided update_token_balance.  
Therefore this is an artificial initial balance.

## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The deployment of interchain tokens ought to take into account whether the token id already has some balance on the source chain. If so, the token balance tracking logic should also be started for it -  without forgetting to take the amount of tokens that already exist on the source chain into account.


## Assessed type

Context

raw_row.title: Users can deploy gateway tokens but they won't work properly

title: Users can deploy gateway tokens but they won't work properly
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L294
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L707


# Vulnerability details

## Description
The deployTokenManager function at the InterchainTokenService contract only stops callers from deploying NATIVE_INTERCHAIN_TOKEN token managers:
```solidity
if (tokenManagerType == TokenManagerType.NATIVE_INTERCHAIN_TOKEN) revert CannotDeploy(tokenManagerType);
```

If a user deploys a gateway token manager, the `_checkPayloadAgainstGatewayData` function will always revert as the gateway tokens deployed by users in a permissionless fashion do not necessarily have a stored symbol at the gateway:
```solidity
function _checkPayloadAgainstGatewayData(bytes memory payload, string calldata tokenSymbol, uint256 amount) internal view {
        ...
        if (validTokenAddress(tokenId) != gateway.tokenAddresses(tokenSymbol) || amount != amountInPayload)
            revert InvalidGatewayTokenTransfer(tokenId, payload, tokenSymbol, amount);
    }
```
Since the gateway is protocol-controlled, stored symbols is not likely to be an offering for retail users. 

The `_checkPayloadAgainstGatewayData` function is executed in both the contractCallWithTokenValue and expressExecuteWithToken functions - that are crucial for the usage of a gateway token.  Since both coordinate the flow of cross-chain token messaging, the gateway token managers deployed by users do not deliver its core functionality.

## Impact
Gateway tokens deployed by users are unusable. 
Users may deploy gateway token managers at the original chain believing its supposed to work properly, but it doesn't.
## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Make sure to disallow users from deploying gateway token managers at the deployTokenManager function. 
The registerGatewayToken function at the factory contract already helps in solving the issue  as it only allows the contract owner to call deployTokenManager for a gateway token manager.
The next step in ensuring gateway token managers cannot be deployed by other users is ensuring only deployTokenManager calls made by the factory contract can deploy token managers of the gateway type:
```solidity
function deployTokenManager(
        bytes32 salt,
        string calldata destinationChain,
        TokenManagerType tokenManagerType,
        bytes calldata params,
        uint256 gasValue
    ) external payable whenNotPaused returns (bytes32 tokenId) {
    ...
	if (msg.sender != interchainTokenFactory){
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `callContract` function in the `BaseAmplifierGateway.sol` contract doesn't perform any validation on its input parameters. This lack of input validation can lead to several potential issues:

1. **Invalid Data**: Without validation, the function can accept invalid or malformed data, which could lead to unexpected behavior or errors in the contract.
2. **Security Risks**: Malicious actors could exploit the lack of validation to pass harmful data, potentially leading to vulnerabilities such as reentrancy attacks or data corruption.
3. **Operational Failures**: Invalid input data could cause the function to fail or behave unpredictably, impacting the reliability and correctness of the contract.

## Proof of Concept
The vulnerable code is located in the `callContract` function:

```solidity
function callContract(
    string calldata destinationChain,
    string calldata destinationContractAddress,
    bytes calldata payload
) external {
    emit ContractCall(msg.sender, destinationChain, destinationContractAddress, keccak256(payload), payload);
}
```

### Example Scenario
1. **Invalid `destinationChain`**: If an invalid or non-existent chain name is passed as `destinationChain`, the function will still emit an event, but the intended cross-chain communication may fail.
2. **Empty `destinationContractAddress`**: If an empty string is passed as `destinationContractAddress`, the function will still proceed, potentially leading to failed transactions or unintended behavior.
3. **Malformed `payload`**: If a malformed payload is passed, it could lead to unexpected behavior when the payload is processed on the destination chain.

## Tools Used
Manual code review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To mitigate this vulnerability, implement input validation checks to ensure that the parameters passed to the `callContract` function are valid and meet the expected criteria. Here are some recommended steps:

1. **Validate `destinationChain`**: Ensure that the `destinationChain` parameter is a valid and registered chain name.

```solidity
require(bytes(destinationChain).length > 0, "Invalid destination chain");
```

2. **Validate `destinationContractAddress`**: Ensure that the `destinationContractAddress` parameter is not empty and follows the expected format for contract addresses.

```solidity
require(bytes(destinationContractAddress).length > 0, "Invalid destination contract address");
```

3. **Validate `payload`**: Ensure that the `payload` parameter is not empty and meets any specific criteria required for the payload data.

```solidity
require(payload.length > 0, "Invalid payload");
```

### Updated `callContract` Function
Here is an updated version of the `callContract` function with input validation:

```solidity
function callContract(
    string calldata destinationChain,
    string calldata destinationContractAddress,
    bytes calldata payload
) external {
    require(bytes(destinationChain).length > 0, "Invalid destination chain");
    require(bytes(destinationContractAddress).length > 0, "Invalid destination contract address");
    require(payload.length > 0, "Invalid payload");

    emit ContractCall(msg.sender, destinationChain, destinationContractAddress, keccak256(payload), payload);
}
```

By implementing these validation checks, you can ensure that the `callContract` function only processes valid and well-formed input data, reducing the risk of unexpected behavior, security vulnerabilities, and operational failures.

In the `execute_message` function, there is a potential logic bug related to a missed check:

The function verifies that the source address matches the trusted address for the source chain, but it does not verify that the destination chain in the message matches the current chain (config.chain_name). This bug breaks the fundamental assumption of correct message routing in the cross-chain system.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact


The logic bug in the `route_incoming_messages` function is in the message verification process. The function checks if each incoming message exists in storage and matches the stored message, but it does not actually verify that the message has been approved or is ready for routing.

Specifically:
1. It only checks if the message exists and matches, but not its status.
2. There's no check to ensure the message has been properly verified before routing.
3. It allows routing of messages that may still be pending verification.

To fix this, the function should:
1. Check the status of each message (e.g., verified, pending, rejected).
2. Only allow routing of messages that have been fully verified and approved.
3. Reject or postpone routing for messages that are still pending or have been rejected.

This oversight could potentially allow unverified or unapproved messages to be routed, compromising the security and integrity of the cross-chain communication system.

## Proof of Concept

2. Messages are saved in `incoming_msg` storage upon `call_contract`, without verification.
3. `route_incoming_messages` can be called by anyone, not just the router.

Impact and PoC:
1. Attacker calls `call_contract` with malicious payload, which saves the message.
2. Attacker immediately calls `route_incoming_messages` with the same message.
3. The function finds the message in storage and routes it without verification.
4. This bypasses the entire verification process (Voting Verifier, etc.).
5. Malicious message gets routed to the destination chain via the router.

The `ExecuteMsg::UpdateTrustedAddress` message in the ITS Hub contract requires `Elevated` permissions, meaning only addresses with `Admin` or `Governance` roles can execute this message. However, the admin and governance addresses are never set in the ITS Hub contract.

## Impact
Trusted addresses can never be added or updated, which would result in the ITS Hub being unable to handle ITS messages from source addresses that aren't set as trusted addresses during the contract's instantiation. Additionally, if a trusted address becomes compromised on a chain then it can't be updated, which further compromises the security and functionality.

## Proof of Concept
`ExecuteMsg::UpdateTrustedAddress` requires `Elevated = (Permission::Admin | Permission::Governance)` permission:
```rust
#[cw_serde]
#[derive(EnsurePermissions)]
pub enum ExecuteMsg {
    #[permission(Specific(gateway))]
    Execute {
        cc_id: CrossChainId,
        source_address: Address,
        payload: HexBinary,
    },
@>  #[permission(Elevated)]
    UpdateTrustedAddress { chain: ChainName, address: Address },
}
```
```rust
flags! {
    #[repr(u8)]
    #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
    pub enum Permission: u8 {
        NoPrivilege = 0b001, // this specifies that the user MUST NOT have an elevated role
        Admin = 0b010,
        Governance = 0b100,
@>      Elevated = (Permission::Admin | Permission::Governance).bits(),
        Any = (Permission::NoPrivilege | Permission::Elevated).bits(),
    }
}
```
Permissions are enforced when calling `execute` on the ITS Hub contract:
```rust
#[cfg_attr(not(feature = "library"), entry_point)]
pub fn execute(
    deps: DepsMut,
    _: Env,
    info: MessageInfo,
    msg: ExecuteMsg,
) -> Result<Response, axelar_wasm_std::error::ContractError> {
@>  let msg = msg.ensure_permissions(deps.storage, &info.sender, match_gateway)?;
    ...
}
```

```rust
const ADMIN: Item<Addr> = Item::new("permission_control_contract_admin_addr");

const GOVERNANCE: Item<Addr> = Item::new("permission_control_governance_addr");

pub fn set_admin(storage: &mut dyn cosmwasm_std::Storage, addr: &Addr) -> StdResult<()> {
    ADMIN.save(storage, addr)
}

pub fn set_governance(storage: &mut dyn cosmwasm_std::Storage, addr: &Addr) -> StdResult<()> {
    GOVERNANCE.save(storage, addr)
}
```

Add that the `instantiate` function calls `permission_control::set_admin` and/or `permission_control::set_governance`. Additionally, consider implementing the ability to update the admin/governance addresses.

```javascript
===>        .add_event(AxelarnetGatewayEvent::MessageExecuted { msg }.into()))
}
```

The `add_message` function is responsible for pushing the now `EXECUTED` messages into a list of messages to be processed:

```javascript
 /// This creates a "fire and forget" message, by using `SubMsg::new()` to wrap it,
    /// and adds it to the list of messages to process.
    pub fn add_message(mut self, msg: impl Into<CosmosMsg<T>>) -> Self {
        self.messages.push(SubMsg::new(msg));
        self
    }
```

There is a discrepancy, however, between message status and actual processing. Messages are labeled as `EXECUTED` while still pending in the processing queue. As per the [Axelar Docs](https://docs.axelar.dev/dev/general-message-passing/monitoring):  `EXECUTED: informs the executed result whether it is successful or not.` In reality, messages marked as `EXECUTED` may still be awaiting processing and are therefore not finalised. 

As for the event, it will emit a `MessageExecuted` event, even though the message might still be in the processing phase and, in some cases, could remain stuck for a while. Despite this, the event will still indicate that the message has been executed.

As per the [README](https://code4rena.com/audits/2024-08-axelar-network#top):

```
- Does the message validation function accurately validate messages and update their status?
```

We believe our finding showcases that the message validation can reflect an incorrect status. 
### Recommendation
We recommend introducing logic that accurately reflects the state of a message when it is still in processing mode.


## Assessed type

Other

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/gateway/AxelarAmplifierGateway.sol#L80-L86


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The approveMessages function allows any user to call it and submit a valid proof to approve messages. If a user obtains or observes a valid proof, they can submit the proof on-chain, potentially leading to unauthorized message approvals.

## Proof of Concept
The vulnerability is present in the following section of the contract:
[AxelarAmplifierGateway.sol Line 80-86](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/gateway/AxelarAmplifierGateway.sol#L80-L86)
**No Access Control:** The `approveMessages` function is `external` and lacks any access control, meaning anyone can call it as long as they have a valid proof.

**Example Code Flow:**
1. An attacker monitors the network for valid proofs or exploits an off-chain vulnerability to obtain one.
2. The attacker calls the `approveMessages` function with the valid proof.
3. The `_validateProof` function checks the proof and verifies the signatures, but since there's no restriction on who can call the function, the attacker's call succeeds.
4. The `_approveMessages` function is then executed, approving the messages and potentially triggering unauthorized cross-chain transactions.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
**Add Access Control**: Restrict the `approveMessages` function so that only authorized entities, such as specific roles or the operator, can call it. This can be done using OpenZeppelin’s `AccessControl` or by implementing a custom role management

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/gateway/BaseAmplifierGateway.sol#L174


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

- The vulnerability allows an attacker to reuse valid signatures from a previous epoch, bypassing the intended security checks. This enables the execution of unauthorized transactions, potentially compromising the integrity and security of the entire multisig system. If exploited, the attacker could perform malicious actions such as unauthorized fund transfers, contract modifications, or any other critical operations that rely on multisig approval.

## Proof of Concept
Explanation:

 -   Initialization and Retention Setting:
        During contract deployment, the previousSignersRetention parameter is set, determining how many previous signer sets are considered valid.
        If this value is greater than 0, older signers can still authorize transactions, leading to the vulnerability.

-    Validation Logic in _validateProof Function:
        The _validateProof function checks the validity of signatures by comparing them against the signer set of the current or any previous epoch within the retention limit.
        The code fails to distinguish between the latest epoch's signers and those from previous epochs, provided the proof meets the required threshold.

-    Signature Replay Attack:
        An attacker can capture valid signatures from a previous epoch and reuse them within the valid retention period.
        Due to the lack of strict enforcement of current epoch signatures, the contract accepts these outdated signatures as valid, allowing unauthorized actions.

Steps to Reproduce:

-    Deploy the Contract:
        Set previousSignersRetention to a value greater than 0.

-    Generate and Capture Signatures:
        Capture a valid signature from an authorized transaction during the initial epoch.

-    Epoch Rotation:
        Rotate signers to a new epoch, updating the signer set.

-    Replay the Captured Signature:
        Use the captured signature from the previous epoch to authorize a new transaction.
-        Observe that the contract accepts this outdated signature, executing the transaction without the approval of the current signers.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

-    Enforce Strict Epoch Validation:
        Modify the _validateProof function to ensure that only signatures from the latest signer set (current epoch) are accepted.
        Reject any signatures associated with outdated epochs, even if they fall within the previousSignersRetention window.

-    Signature Invalidation Post-Rotation:
        Implement logic to invalidate or mark as stale any signatures once an epoch rotation occurs, rendering them unusable even if retained for historical purposes.




## Assessed type

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/69c4f2c3fcefb1b8eb2129af9c3685a44ae5b6fe/axelar-gmp-sdk-solidity/contracts/gateway/AxelarAmplifierGateway.sol#L101-L103


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details
As the developer comments state in `rotateSigners`: `The gateway operator allows recovery in case of an incorrect/malicious rotation, while still requiring a valid proof from a recent signer set.`. The issue is that there are edge-cases in which the operator will be unable to prevent a malicious rotation. It is important to add that the protocol team has stated on the contest's page that this is a valid functional concern: [Can the signer rotation function address potential edge cases and ensure proper updates to the signer set?](https://code4rena.com/audits/2024-08-axelar-network#top:~:text=Can%20the%20signer%20rotation%20function%20address%20potential%20edge%20cases%20and%20ensure%20proper%20updates%20to%20the%20signer%20set%3F)

## Impact
If any of the three attacks, provided in `Proof of Concept`, occur `AmplifierGateway` will be entirely under the control of malicious signers and invalid/harmful messages will be approved.


## Proof of Concept
Here are the possible edge-cases:

1/ A set of malicious signers is able to call `rotateSigners` with addresses under their control `previousSignersRetention` times. Now all possible sets of signers that the operator can use to call `rotateSigners` will be controlled by the initial set of malicious signers. Thus, the malicious signers are completely free to approve any harmful messages without the danger of being rotated by the operator.

2/ If the first rotation of signers is malicious the operator will be unable to rotate to a different set of signers. This happens as the only way for `_validateProof` to not revert will be if the malicious set of signers approves the rotation, which will not occur.

3/ If `previousSignersRetention` is set to 0 the operator will again need the signatures of the malicious signers, which will be unsuccessful as explained in the previous point.

It is important to note that `previousSignersRetention` is immutable and the operator will not be able to increase it to prevent an attack.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
There are multiple ways to resolve the issue, one is to allow the operator or owner to rotate the signers in case of an attack without the need for signatures of previous signers.





## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/69c4f2c3fcefb1b8eb2129af9c3685a44ae5b6fe/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L663


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details
The purpose of the `contractCallWithTokenValue` function is: `Returns the amount of token that this call is worth`. The issue is that in order for a user to get the amount, they are looking for, they need to supply the same amount. This is contradictory to the entire purpose of the function and users will be unable to get the value they are looking for.

This function is important as stated by the protocol team: `These functions are queried by the express relayer to determine the value of the ITS call. They are not the main focus of the audit but support the relayer in processing transactions.` Therefore, the express relayer will be hurdled in determining the value of an ITS contract call with token.

## Impact
Due to issues in the logic of the `contractCallWithTokenValue` function, it will be practically unusable.

## Proof of Concept
As we can see in the code, `contractCallWithTokenValue` makes a call to `_checkPayloadAgainstGatewayData`:

```solidity
function contractCallWithTokenValue(
        string calldata sourceChain,
        string calldata sourceAddress,
        bytes calldata payload,
        string calldata symbol,
        uint256 amount
    ) public view virtual onlyRemoteService(sourceChain, sourceAddress) whenNotPaused returns (address, uint256) {
        _checkPayloadAgainstGatewayData(payload, symbol, amount);
        return _contractCallValue(payload);
    }
```

This is problematic, as `_checkPayloadAgainstGatewayData` requires the caller to supply `amount` as a parameter. The `amount` that the user needs to supply is the same as the `amount` that they are querying the function for, contradictory to the purpose of the function.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The `_checkPayloadAgainstGatewayData` in `contractCallWithTokenValue` is practically not needed and can be omitted.








## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network/blob/4572617124bed39add9025317d2c326acfef29f1/interchain-token-service/contracts/InterchainTokenService.sol#L632-L643


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details
Currently, in order for tokens to be transferred from one chain to another they first need to be locked/burnt on the source chain and then unlocked/minted on the destination chain. The issue is that there are several cases where the tokens will not be able to be recovered on the destination chain, causing a loss of funds for users.

## Impact
Due to the lack of a recovery function for stuck funds, users may suffer a loss of their bridged funds.

## Proof of Concept
Here are the possible scenarios where recovering tokens on the destination chain will be impossible:

1/ If the `flowLimit` becomes less than the transferred funds, before the token bridge has been executed on the destination chain, the initiator of the token transfer will not be able to recover their funds on the destination chain. The only way for this to happen would be if the `flowLimit` is increased to a value higher than the amount of tokens. This may not occur, as it will be fully dependent on the token manager operator, which may be malicious.

2/ If a `TokenManager`, corresponding to the source `tokenId`, has not been deployed on the destination chain it will be impossible for the tokens to be transferred to the destination address, as `TokenHandler.giveToken` will fail.

3/ If a destination chain changes or entirely removes another chain's trusted address, all pending transfers coming from that chain will not be executable. This will prevent users who have transferred tokens from the updated/removed chain and are yet to claim them, from ever retrieving their funds. 
This becomes much more dangerous as with the addition of the ITS Hub, many chains will change their `InterchainAddressTracker` configurations.

4/ There may not be enough locked tokens on the destination chain to transfer to the destination address. This will prevent the user from receiving their bridged tokens until more tokens are locked on the destination chain, which may never happen.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add a recovery mechanism for stuck tokens on the source chain.














## Assessed type

Other

# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details
It is stated on the competition's page that rebasing/deflationary/inflationary tokens should be supported and are [In scope](https://code4rena.com/audits/2024-08-axelar-network#top:~:text=Balance%20changes%20outside,In%20scope). However, the transfer of such tokens through ITS will be dangerous and will cause errors in the protocols accounting balance, causing users to get more funds than intended or some users being unable to claim their transferred tokens of the destination chain.

## Impact
Loss of funds for users of the protocol and accounting errors in the ITS.

## Proof of Concept
If rebasing tokens are transferred through the ITS the following issue is likely to arise:
1/ User transfers 1000 of a rebasing token from chain A to chain B, so 1000 tokens are locked in the `TokenManager` for the token on chain A
2/ Before the transfer is executed on chain B the token rebases, decreasing balances by 10%
3/ The user finishes the bridging on chain B and receives 1000 tokens, even though they should have only received 900
4/ The 100 tokens that are added to the user are taken out of other users' locked tokens, causing further accounting issues

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
One long-term solution would be to implement a special `TokenManager` contract designed for handling rebasing tokens.

ERC20
